body.question: What did I write about ArrayList vs LinkedList?

response:
{"id":4,"answer":"What you saved on this is a single short note, so here it is in full plus what it leaves out.

From your notes
- Your note (id 3) says: ArrayList gives O(1) random access because it is backed by an array; LinkedList is O(n) for get(i) but O(1) insert/remove at the ends.
- You also flagged that you keep mixing these two up for your DSA exam, so this is a known weak spot rather than settled knowledge.

General knowledge (not in your notes) — the usual caveats
- Backing structure: ArrayList wraps a resizable Object[]; LinkedList is a doubly-linked list of nodes, each holding prev/next pointers plus the element.
- Middle operations: ArrayList add/remove at an arbitrary index is O(n) because elements shift; LinkedList is O(1) only if you already hold the node (e.g. via an iterator/ListIterator) — finding that node by index is still O(n).
- End operations are subtly asymmetric: ArrayList append is amortized O(1) (grows by ~1.5x), but remove(0) is O(n). LinkedList addFirst/removeFirst is genuinely O(1).
- Memory and speed in practice: LinkedList has per-node object overhead and poor cache locality, so on real hardware ArrayList often wins even for workloads the Big-O table favours LinkedList for. Many sources say LinkedList is rarely the right default.
- Interfaces: LinkedList also implements Deque (so it doubles as a queue/stack); ArrayList does not.

Tiny code-shaped example
    List<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>();
    a.get(500);              // O(1)
    a.add(0, 7);             // O(n) shift

    LinkedList<Integer> l = new LinkedList<>();
    l.addFirst(7);           // O(1)
    l.get(500);              // O(n) walk
    l.removeFirst();         // O(1), ArrayList.remove(0) is O(n)

If you want a one-line rule: index-heavy reads -> ArrayList; frequent add/remove at the head or a queue-like workload -> ArrayDeque (usually preferred over LinkedList) or LinkedList for its Deque behaviour.","references":{"coverage":"partial","general_knowledge":true,"explanation":"Only one saved note (id 3) directly answers this question, and it is brief — two complexity claims plus a note that you mix the two up — so coverage is partial rather than sufficient.
